paragraphs.text: Great matters need great narratives, and the illustrious histories of the righteous need an illustrious tongue and mind: a mind that contemplates the divine Scriptures with purity, and a tongue that interprets divine things clearly. This is above all true of the subject before us, I mean the trials endured by blessed Job, which, spreading through all the earth under heaven, make the message of endurance shine out. Yet even if the account of this subject is beyond our weakness, I know well that the grace of God supplies speech, not because of the worth of the speaker but because of the intercession of the fathers. But let us come to the narrative itself: “There was a man in the land of Ausitis.” First we must consider what force the opening has, and why the historian began with this phrase: “There was a man.” He was about to narrate a virtuous life, one far surpassing our condition. So that no one, looking at the extraordinary greatness of his contests, should think his nature foreign and not human, he showed his nature beforehand, so that you might marvel at his resolve: that, being a man, he lived above man, sharing a nature common to all, yet lifting his soul higher than the world. “There was a man in the land of Ausitis.” He proclaims him by his nature, and he proclaims him by his land as well. Just as, on hearing that he was a man, you marvel that he lived above man, so too, when you learn the land from which such fruit blossomed, you may truly marvel at what kind of rose sprang up amid the thorns. Pay close attention. The land of Ausitis, then, was the land of Esau, for Ausitis comes from Esau. He names the land of profane and wicked Esau (as the Apostle says, “Let no one be a fornicator or profane, like Esau”) so that you may marvel at what kind of fruit of truth blossomed from such schools of wickedness. And it was not only the land of Esau that brought him forth, but the very root of Esau, for he was a descendant of that reproached man. For Scripture says that Job was fifth from Abraham. Hear how he was fifth: Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Esau, Esau begot Reuel, Reuel begot Zerah, and Zerah begot Job. So his line of descent came down to him from Abraham through Esau. He shows the root, then, so that you may marvel at the fruit. Who was Esau? A fornicator and profane. And who was Job? The one sprung from the fornicator, this same holy and wonderful man who is now set before us for our narrative, who says: “If my eye has followed another man’s wife, then let my wife also please another man.” Esau had intercourse with many women, insatiable in licentiousness, but Job made his character the law of his life. He held back so far that he did not let himself dwell on beauty that belonged to another, and he kept so far from fornication and adultery that he paid no attention even to women not yet promised in marriage, that is, to unbetrothed virgins. For I must use plainer language: so far was he from plotting against other men’s marriages that he did not cast a lustful eye even on an unbetrothed virgin, where there was no danger. And who testifies to this? Job himself: “I made a covenant with my eyes,” he says, “and I did not give thought to a virgin.” See to what degree of discipline his piety came to flower in him. He trains his eye to piety, he trains his members to righteousness, and though he bore descent from the fornicator, he shone with the greatest chastity. Esau was also a fratricide, as far as intention goes; for even if the deed did not come to pass, the intention stands condemned. For Esau said in his heart, it says, “Let the days of mourning for my father draw near, and I will kill my brother Jacob.” The root, then, was fratricidal, but the one who blossomed from the root was an umpire of righteousness. The one made war on nature and treated his brother as a stranger; this one regarded even strangers as brothers, saying: “I became like a father to orphans, and in place of a husband to their mother. The case I did not know I searched out, and I put an end to the unjust.” So he makes everything that belongs to others his own concern, though he bore descent from Esau, who made what belonged to others his own. Esau plotted in his mind to kill Jacob, but Job offered sacrifices for his sons, thinking that they might perhaps have sinned in thought. Since Esau had planned murder in his mind, this great and noble athlete feared that his sons too might admit the poison of sin into their thoughts, and so he offered a sacrifice, and one calf for sins. For Job said: “Perhaps my sons have thought evil against God?” Consider to what exactness the training of his character had reached. And what does he do? Their forebears Esau and Jacob had become enemies to one another, not because Jacob joined in wickedness, but because Esau began it. So he dissolves the discord of the forebears by feasting, and makes his sons feast with one another day by day, so that the shared table might dissolve the poison of wickedness. Job’s sons visited one another, trained in harmony from a young age, practicing peace and learning concord, and they ate and drank together. And they also invited, it says, their three sisters to eat and drink with them. What benefit is this to the listener? And why did he add that the sisters feasted with them? To show how self-controlled their banquet was, and that there was no disorderly, unrestrained laughter and no licentiousness insulting the table. That is why he brings in the virgins feasting too: to show that the character of the banquet was not disgraced by drunkenness but crowned with concord. “There was a man in the land of Ausitis”: a dove among hawks, a sheep among wolves, a star among the clouds, a lily among thorns, the shoot of righteousness in the village of unrighteousness. “And that man was blameless.”

Pay close attention. Those outside the faith have laid down a definition of man. What is man? “Man,” they say, “is a rational, mortal animal.” That is what the philosophers’ definitions say. But Scripture does not give definitions of that kind. What does it give? A man blameless, righteous, true. If anyone asks you and demands a definition of what man is, tell him: “Blameless, righteous, true, abstaining from every evil deed.” For one who is not attested by such achievements is not even a man. If he has the stamp of human nature but outrages it by the wickedness of his choices, he hears from the prophet: “Man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them.” “And that man was blameless.” This is no small praise. Examine the word closely, so that you may marvel at his resolve. A charge is one thing and blame another: a charge is brought for the gravest sins, while blame arises over the slightest faults. So the writer wanted to show that the righteous man was far not only from charges but also from blame. No one charged him with doing great wrongs, since no one even blamed him for doing small ones. This is a great proof, for a life that is merely free of charges is only middling. Someone you cannot charge with adultery or murder is free of charges; but someone you blame for insolence, slander, abuse or drunkenness, though beyond the reach of charges, still falls under blame. So he wanted to show that Job was far even from small and very slight faults, and he says: “He was blameless, righteous, true, God-fearing, abstaining from every evil deed.” Hence God too, wishing to show Abraham that the first thing in virtue is blamelessness, says to him: “Be well-pleasing before me, and be blameless.” “Blameless” is understood as the summit of character. But the apostle Paul did not add this summit of virtue, because among the Gentiles he had people torn away from polytheism, gathered out of wickedness, collected from fornication and adultery. When he came into a world full of fornication and adultery and wished to appoint shepherds for the world, since the goods of virtue were scarce at that time, he says to Titus about appointing bishops: “Appoint bishops, as I directed you, if anyone is above reproach.” “Blameless” had no place then, since, as I said before, the things of piety were still scarce. Blamelessness is great, being above reproach is middling, but in evil times even a small good is great.

That is why he said, “the husband of one wife.” This is not because that is the standard kept in the church now, for the priest must be crowned with complete purity and holiness. Rather, because it was a great thing at that time compared with those living in fornication, he says: “Appoint bishops, as I directed you, if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife.” He did not lay this down as a law; he made allowance for their error. For he knew that when the message of piety flourished, nature itself would readily choose the good, and the better would be chosen. “Blameless, righteous.” So one cannot become righteous without first becoming blameless. “True.” What does “true” mean? One who does not put on an outward appearance while his inner condition is different; who does not feign chastity while clothed in licentiousness; who does not display righteousness in his bearing while carrying unrighteousness in his heart. Such a man is true, and at once God-fearing. For when there is blamelessness, righteousness and truthfulness, then true fear of God is made complete. “Abstaining from every evil deed.” Many abstain from many sins but not from all; so, wishing again to set before us the summit of virtue, he says: “abstaining from every evil deed.” Hence David also says: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.” For one cannot both fear God and do evil. He also sets out Job’s possessions: he had seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred grazing donkeys. Why does he set these out? Not because he admires Job’s wealth, but to leave you, the listener, with the size of his property, so that when you later see him stripped of his possessions and not groaning, you may marvel that, deprived of so many good things, he does not reject his benefactor and does not insult his Creator. These things were written, then, not so that you might admire the wealth, but so that you might praise the perseverance and endurance of the righteous man and always keep the fear of God before your eyes. But the rest of the passage will keep its exposition for another time. For the devil, brothers, saw Job rich with this temporary wealth, and saw him storing up eternal wealth from this temporary wealth, and he reasoned that just as righteousness had grown rich along with him while he was rich, so virtue too would grow poor along with him once he was poor. So he tries to strip him of his money, in order to strip him of his virtues as well. Here let those pay close attention who say: “Wasn’t Job rich? Wasn’t Abraham rich? Why then do you urge poverty on us?” I in turn will say to you: Be rich like Job, and I pray that you acquire still more. Be like Abraham, and the whole earth will join in praying for your wealth. Say, as Job did: “My door was open to everyone in distress.” Say: “I warmed the shoulders of the poor.” Say: “The shoulders of the poor were warmed by the fleece of my sheep.” Say: “And the mouth of the widow blessed me.” Then be as rich as you like. For you will be found not rich for yourself but a steward for the poor. “My door,” he says, “was open to everyone in distress.” Imitate the height of this love for the poor. Put on zeal for endurance, stand like a man against adversity, and keep an even mind in all things. But enough of this for now. May it be granted that we, holding on to this zeal and endurance, keep fresh in mind the rest of the passage that remains, that you demand the remainder from us, and that we pay you the continuation of these reflections. And may it be granted us to celebrate the feast sincerely, and, having shared in the sufferings of the saints, to share also in the passion of Christ. For truly, brothers, it was right that the sufferings of the saints shone out before the passion of Christ. The sufferings of the righteous flashed out beforehand like lightning, so that afterward Christ might appear, as Paul says, who suffers with all and is glorified with all. So, by the prayers and intercessions of the holy fathers, keeping in step with what has been said and awaiting what remains, let us send up glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
